name: Machboos
description: Rice cooked in a spiced broth with chicken, lamb or fish (hammour or kingfish) and loomi (dried lime). Known across the Gulf as kabsa or machboos, it is served at Emirati family gatherings and is often compared to biryani.
how_to_eat: Eat with the meat on top of the rice, ideally shared from one platter.
how_to_order: Ask for 'machboos' with chicken, lamb or fish at Emirati restaurants.

name: Harees
description: Wheat and meat slow-cooked for hours into a smooth porridge, topped with ghee. It is most common during Ramadan.
how_to_eat: Eat with a spoon while hot.
how_to_order: Ask for 'harees' at Emirati restaurants, especially during Ramadan.

name: Thareed
description: Lamb or chicken stewed with vegetables in spiced broth and poured over layers of thin rigag bread. It is shared from one big dish at weddings, Eid and iftar.
how_to_eat: Eat from the shared dish, scooping the soaked bread with the stew.
how_to_order: Ask for 'thareed' at Emirati restaurants, mainly during Ramadan.

name: Ghuzi
description: A whole lamb slow-roasted and served on rice with nuts, raisins and vegetables. It is a feast dish found across the Gulf.
how_to_eat: Share from the platter, pulling the lamb off the bone.
how_to_order: Order 'ghuzi' at Emirati restaurants; it is usually for groups.

name: Luqaimat
description: Small dough balls fried crisp outside and soft inside, drizzled with date syrup or honey and sometimes rolled in sesame. They are eaten hot and are especially popular in Ramadan.
how_to_order: Buy a portion from Emirati restaurants or the stalls at Global Village.

name: Balaleet
description: Vermicelli sweetened with sugar, cardamom, rose water and saffron, served under a thin omelette. It is a popular Emirati breakfast and the first meal of Eid al-Fitr.
how_to_eat: Eat the sweet noodles and egg together.
how_to_order: Ask for 'balaleet' at breakfast in Emirati cafés.

name: Chabab
description: A yeasted Emirati pancake flavoured with cardamom and saffron. It is a breakfast bread served with honey, date syrup or cheese.
how_to_eat: Eat warm with date syrup or cheese.
how_to_order: Ask for 'chabab' at breakfast in Emirati cafés.

name: Regag
description: A paper-thin, crispy Emirati flatbread cooked on a hot plate and topped with egg, cheese and sometimes honey. It is a breakfast staple.
how_to_eat: Eat folded, right off the griddle.
how_to_order: Ask for 'regag' with egg and cheese at Emirati breakfast spots.

name: Gahwa
description: Light Arabic coffee brewed with cardamom and served in small handleless cups with dates. It is the UAE's gesture of welcome.
how_to_eat: Drink in small sips with dates.
how_to_order: It is offered free at homes, hotels and offices; cafés also serve it with dates.

name: Dubai Chocolate
description: A milk chocolate bar filled with pistachio-tahini cream and crunchy chopped kadayif, inspired by knafeh. It was devised in 2021 and first sold in 2022 by Dubai's Fix Dessert Chocolatier, and went viral worldwide in 2024.
how_to_eat: Break it to hear the crunch of the kadayif filling.
how_to_order: Buy from chocolatiers and cafés in Dubai.

name: Karak Chai
description: Strong black tea boiled with milk and sugar, a drink popularised in the Gulf by South Asian migrants. It is a UAE staple, sold cheaply at cafeterias and drive-up counters.
how_to_eat: Drink hot, often right in the car from a drive-up cafeteria.
how_to_order: Ask for 'karak' at any cafeteria; neighbourhood cafeterias charge from about 1-2.50 AED a cup.

name: Shawarma
description: Spit-roasted chicken, lamb or beef shaved into pita with salad and garlic sauce or tahini. Originally from the Levant, it is one of the most popular street foods in Dubai and across the UAE.
how_to_eat: Eat as a wrap on the go.
how_to_order: Ask for chicken or meat shawarma at any shawarma counter.

name: Khameer
description: A traditional Emirati breakfast bread, cooked like ragag and chebab on a curved hot plate first used by the Bedouins. It is served with cheese, date syrup or eggs.
how_to_eat: Eat warm at breakfast with cheese, date syrup or eggs.
how_to_order: Ask for 'khameer' bread at Emirati breakfast spots.

name: Khanfaroosh
description: A popular Gulf sweet made from rice flour, wheat flour, sugar, eggs and water mixed into a batter and deep-fried. Saffron, cardamom, rose water or milk are often added for flavour.
how_to_order: Ask for 'khanfaroosh' where Emirati sweets are sold.

name: Jasheed
description: A coastal Emirati curry of small pieces of shark (or other local fish) cooked with onions, garlic and spices, served with rice. It is mainly eaten in coastal cities such as Ras Al Khaimah.
how_to_order: Ask for 'jasheed' at Emirati seafood restaurants.

name: Khabeesa
description: An Emirati dessert of toasted flour (or bread crumbs) cooked with water, sugar, saffron and cardamom until thick. It is finished covered over coals for about half an hour.
how_to_order: Ask for 'khabeesa' where traditional Emirati desserts are served.

name: Bethitha
description: One of the best-known Emirati sweets: flour or semolina toasted until reddish, then mixed with butter, crushed dates and cardamom. It is simple to prepare and served as is.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bethitha' where traditional Emirati desserts are served.

name: Khubz mohalla
description: A round Emirati bread like ragag, cooked on both sides on a ghee-greased hot plate until brown. It can be topped with egg and is served on a big plate with honey.
how_to_order: Ask for 'khubz mohalla' at Emirati breakfast spots.

name: Al-qurs al-mafrook
description: A traditional Emirati dish, popular in winter, of dough made from flour, salt, ghee and dates, baked in a large round among embers. It is then broken up and rubbed with ghee, and topped with honey or sugar.
how_to_order: Ask for 'qurs mafrook' where traditional Emirati food is served.
